utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. If there's nothing else to be discussed at this moment, we could ask Madam Usher to accompany Mr. Kirudja into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kirudja.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President and Your Honours; good morning, counsel; good morning, Mr. Kirudja.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no questions of Mr. Kirudja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge El Mahdi has one or more questions for you. Questioned by the Court: JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Kirudja. I would like to ask you some further questions. First of all, you told us that your mandate, i.e., the UN mandate, was split between four sectors and that you were in charge of Sector North. Did you hold meetings between various sector representatives?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, we did. My counterpart -- there were CACs, civil affairs coordinators, for each sector. Once every so on, it wasn't as regular as it might look, but we were invited by the director, Mr. Thornberry, back to Zagreb as heads of those sectors, and we would discuss matters that were common to all sectors. More often, however - I forget the frequency but it was much more frequent - the force commander held meetings in Zagreb where more than civil affairs coordinators would meet, where all the heads, the military, the civilian, and police, will meet in a much bigger conference chaired by the force commander. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [No interpretation] [Interpretation] The departure of the non-Serbs from neighbouring areas and the areas bordering Sector North had been planned, so to speak. Did the sector representatives of the other sectors share your point of view, because you exchanged your views, didn't you, with others?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did exchange our experience, our analysis, and our comments with the other representatives from other sectors. Your question also contained the question that did the other sectors share similar points of view or analysis. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The other sectors had quite different experiences, mainly because of their locations, especially Sector East. If you remember the first map that we presented, its location had different dynamics. Sector West had even more special issues. Sector South again had a different issue. So when you look at it overall, we ended up being unique in regard to the issues we discussed the last few days over the forced evacuation of massive numbers of refugees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but may I just intervene for a very technical reason. I see on my screen that from 9:14, that means that a few words of your last question were not translated on the screen. Since I was listening to the live channel rather than to the English translation, I do not know whether it was actually translated and just not on our screen or that it has not been translated. That was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first part wasn't but I understood it in French, the part that wasn't translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I saw from your statement, Mr. Kirudja, the language is not a problem for you, but we need a full transcript. I wonder whether this will be recovered from the tapes. Yes, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I suggest, Your Honour, that it may be, with respect, that His Honour Judge El Mahdi could repeat his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I had in mind. If there are no other ways --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It seems the more sensible thing. I believe he knows his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Judge El Mahdi, just once again. JUDGE EL MAHDI: Thank you, Mr. President. [Interpretation] I shall repeat my question. It concerned those meetings which you held with those people mandated by the UN and in charge of the other sectors the eastern sector, the western sector, and the southern sector. And in the course of these meetings, did you have the opportunity to discuss these matters and to exchange your views and to hear assessments of the situation from other people, and did their assessment of the situation, was it in line with yours? In other words, was there any kind of system or plan that aimed at deporting or at inciting non-Serb people to leave part of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, may I ask you whether this would, with the question being repeated, whether your response -- whether your -- whether you would have testified anything different or you just keep to what you said just.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will keep to what I said. I trust Judge El Mahdi had already understood my answer, but I would defer to him if he would like me to repeat. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] No, not at all. I'd just like one further clarification, please. If I look at the map that is in front of me, Sector West is very close to your sector, Sector North, and it seems to me that you said that Sector West was facing other difficulties, not the ones you mentioned. Now, as concerns Sector West, was a similar question ever raised concerning Sector West? In other words, any form of deportation or expulsion of a segment of the population?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was often in contact with my counterpart in Sector West, Mr. Gerard Fischer. As a matter of fact, on my way to assignment on Sector North, I did spend time in Sector West, in Daruvar, and then down to the other areas that were troublesome in that sector. There were, if my memory is correct, similar attempt for movement of refugees, not as massively as we discussed and not for similar reasons that we discussed, but the details there I don't have as I would have had for Sector North. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] In that case, can one not assume that this method was being applied in those municipalities which were adjacent to yours, to your sector? In other words, it wasn't a very widespread system.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judge El Mahdi, recall part of the testimony that was heard here was the what I call collusion or working in partnership between the mayor in Sector North and Sector South, particularly the mayor in Dvor. The local Serbs, meaning the Serbs, Croatian Serbs located in Sector West, had a totally different dynamic -- JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Please allow me to interrupt you. Yes, I remember this very well. I remember the conversation you had with the mayor of Dvor and that he wanted you to contact the mayor in Bosnia over the phone, but this was not my question. Was this something which prevailed in some municipalities? In other words, was it a matter of -- of asking the non-Serbs to leave, or was this a more widespread system, something which was being applied to a larger part of Bosnia and Herzegovina? I don't know if my question is clear enough and if you understand my subject of concern.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand your question to mean was this phenomenon widespread and especially in Sector West. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I was beginning to respond to you was that the Sector West had local leadership engaged in a different manner than the local leadership in Sector North. Specifically, the Serb leadership in Sector West had approached their own issues very differently, and I didn't understand them, from talking to my counterpart, wanting to facilitate control of the area of Sector West. In other words, they had earlier than us in Sector North even come to a better understanding with the Croatian authorities about autonomy in the area. So their perspective in what would be happening in the sector was, at least in the early part of the month, very different from the perspective in Sector North. And by that I mean that towards the end of my testimony I did refer to the Republic of Serbian Krajina now becoming a very well recognised reality. That recognition was much more strong in Sector North and Sector South than it was in Sector West. Therefore, the ability to -- to organise massive movement from inside Sector North and across the border in Sector West, I never understood that to be as strong as it was in Sector North. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Fine. So in the course of your meetings, the assessment of the situation and the conclusions you drew, had these been vetted and well understood by your colleagues and -- in other words, did their points of view and your point of view tally? Did you assess the situation in the same way?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly in those meetings in Zagreb when we met collectively I did explain to them in full about as much as I did explain to this Court about what we were experiencing, and I recall the -- both the force commander and my colleagues in other areas listening attentively but not offering any different views from what they were hearing from me. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Thank you. I should now like to move on to another topic briefly. In your written statement, and I shall quote you in English: [In English] "The fact that we had no mandate in Bosnia increasingly became a flashpoint and a point of friction both on the front lines where we operated and at the UN headquarters to whom we reported." [Interpretation] My question concerns what do you understand, what do you mean when you talk about friction at the UN headquarters?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a sad thing for me in the sense that while I knew they understood my report, meaning those -- some of which you have seen here, including the ones with the titles like "Humanitarian Disasters in the Making," including the outlining of those places we called concentration camps and what was going on there, I knew they understood that this was going on, but because there was that obvious lack of mandate, the UN not at a certain point mandated to operate across the border, rather than respond in the manner I hoped they would, meaning go up the chain from Zagreb and go to where the mandate are created, meaning back at the headquarters, and bring these matters there, I got warnings that you're spending too much time dealing with these issues. In other words, don't look, don't see. The human situation being what it was, I never had that alternative not to see or not to hear what was being brought at the front door of where we were located. Indeed, when they said to me don't get too involved in matters across Bosnia, part of my response was, "We don't even have to go to Bosnia. They come to us inside the sector." That's the friction I'm referring to. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Thank you. Did you feel the weight of the SDS party in the course of those meetings which you held with various members and when you tried to assess the situation?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Beg your pardon, Judge, weight, or pressure, or what exactly? JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Did you feel in any way that the SDS was playing a part in the events that were unfolding? And if you felt and came to realise that the SDS was playing a part, what kind of part was it actually playing?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the testimony I gave, you will recall mentioning that I would ask the people coming to see me to tell me who they were, and therefore I noticed that -- I mean, I did indicate so-and-so presented themselves as representative of the SDS or representative of the SDA, or the mayor would represent himself as the president of the Crisis Committee. The police who came along, of course they were in uniform and they just said they were the chiefs of police. As those conversations went on and after they were repeated a number of times, it became clear that these people were not acting as individuals in their individual capacity to dream up these plans to evacuate massive people. And as you recall the testimony, at certain point we did make them admit this thing was not a voluntary thing. And you will also recall towards the end we had given them no doubt that something you are doing, that the international community will view it in strict displeasure and indeed it could be considered a crime. Even with that warning, they seemed not to be able or willing to stop the process. In other words, they did appear to have all the signs of being driven to undertake this. And the only way, to my mind, they could be driven is they were acting on instructions under a policy drawn by somebody. And since they identified themselves as SDS or members of the militia or what they called, for better terminology, new reality going on and that reality called Republic of Serbia, it was, towards the end, inescapable for me to conclude they were acting under policy or instruction. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes. My last question relates to paragraph 38 of your declaration. Let me quote you. You said it was evident, and you were talking about a particular family which spent the night in a hotel under the protection of the UN police officers. And you said: [In English] "It was evident that the Serb authorities not only did not tolerate their presence, but they also would not guarantee the security of the family..." [Interpretation] Where did you reach this conclusion? When did you reach this conclusion? You said it was evident. How did you reach this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. The evident was almost natural. They were only attempting to cross over by a road through Sector North in the direction of Karlovac. The fact -- the simple fact that they were stopped and couldn't proceed on the road is itself the evidence that they were in jeopardy of being hurt, and they drove off the main road into Tapusko, seeking assistance and saying, "We feel -- we've been stopped too many -- the militia is chasing us, we need protection, and we also need to be escorted out of the sector." That was the evidence. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] In other words, that is what they told you. In -- according to you, if the authorities wanted to detain them, don't you think they could have done so if they had wanted to?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed. As a matter of fact, they could even have forcefully removed our own police and taken them, because our police were not armed. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] In other words, perhaps it was the mob or paramilitary groups that did not report to the authorities that were involved.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Inside the sector, that would not have been possible because the authorities that were from the militia and the others had total control of the area, as I recall I mentioned to you. This was the situation after the war: They had taken control; there were checkpoints almost every few kilometres around, both for ordinary people as well as -- I mean ordinary local people as well as checking any kind of crime. So movement in the sector was quite controlled by the -- by the forces. So the question of irregular -- the crowd doesn't arise inside the sector. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, I have a few -- a few questions as well. The first one about the same family, the Cakar family that you just mentioned -- well, you didn't mention but you spoke about in your response to one of the questions of Judge El Mahdi. You testified that they were under duress. I'd like to have a clarification on the following question: Is my understanding correct that they were confronted with a situation they experienced as duress once they had decided to leave, that is to say on their way out, or were they also under duress when they decided that they wanted to leave? So was it at the basis of their departure or was it that they faced it during their -- during their trip?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A very precise question, Your Honour. At the very beginning of their trip, I wouldn't have the details because the trip originated from across the border.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: So that part of your question I'm not privy to what might have happened. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Unless they said something.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unless they said something. But it's also important, Your Honour, you bear in mind the timing of this incident. This is very early. It is almost the first two weeks, and it took us by surprise. We didn't expect a woman and a child and a man just merely trying to pass through the road to be in such kind of despondency when they arrived literally outside our office first. It drew our attention not merely to the issues you're asking, how they felt in distress, it drew our attention as to who are they and why. And as soon as we established the fact that they are not from here, they are -- and if you use the word "alien" to this group of people here, then the next question was, why not let them out? And then when we started talking to them when they had calmed down, I remember they were in panic, they began to hint that they had been stopped so many times once inside, even between the border to the headquarters - and the only one who could have stopped them were the authorities manning those checkpoints - so we then asked them -- I just went to the authorities and said, "What's the matter with this woman? Why couldn't she continue, or this family, and go where they wanted to go?" And that's when I began to get the idea, and they told us, "These are foreigners. These are non-Serbs, and they shouldn't be here." And that's when then the matter began focusing on their car. The first hint was they can leave but the car cannot leave. And I say, "How can they leave without their own assets?" They would say, "Why don't you put in your UN car and take her out?" "Yes, but these are our properties." And then the issue began to develop around that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yesterday a question was put to you - this is a different subject - on who you would accept as the responsible parties to receive responses to. Especially you talked about the people at the opstina level and the RSK level, and I did understand from your answer that there was some hesitations to receive the point of view of the RSK level where you rather oriented yourself to the people at the opstina level. This was, as far as I understand, mainly about, well, obstruction of or at least non-compliance with what you deemed necessary to perform your duties. If at the RSK level you would have got a unison response to the extent that everyone below that level would meet your requests, would you have had similar hesitations? I mean, was it that you were hesitant because you'd rather have the point of view of each opstina before you would accept that one would not meet your request or your requirements, or would the same have been true if they would have -- at the RSK level they would have said, "We fully agree with you, everything's fine, we'll do whatever you ask." Would you have had similar hesitations?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Interesting question, since I never had that last option.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It didn't all happen very naturally that the RSK had whipped all these other units into their line and policy. This is something they did over time, including changes, very rapid changes for mayors and chiefs of police who were not in compliance to whatever they issued from their RSK headquarters in Knin, which was in Sector South. Indeed, part of the testimony you have in front of you talks of the killing of one of the very independent mayor of Vrgin Most, who had exhibited what I call a sort of independence in dealing with the -- with us, dealing with the issues that were in the Vance Plan and understood that the Vance Plan gave him, the mayor, and the police the only recognition of authority. In an attempt to act that way, we read it that he was eliminated. And soon thereafter, we got into that position that your last question implied, that the RSK did gain total authority over the opstina leadership. And having recognised that de facto they had gained such authority in all opstinas, if I wanted something done, therefore it was impractical for me to insist to deal with the opstinas where I know they will not cross the line coming from Knin, and consequently, I was often in Knin myself talking directly to where I thought the responsible individuals were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if I do understand your answer correctly, you tell Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. us that it was of no use any more to stick to who you consider to be the proper counterparts because the -- you were, as the French say, before a fait accompli that the RSK had taken over the authority.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly, it's fait accompli.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I have a very small question. Let's not spend too much time on it. You said yesterday that from Petrova Gora you could see the city of Zagreb. On the map you provided it seems to be a distance of some 60 kilometres with quite a lot of elevations, even close to the city of Zagreb, I would say a distance of ten to 15 kilometres, and there is an indication on this map that one of the elevation points in Petrova Gora was 572 metres. And if you find close to the city of Zagreb elevations to -- up to 265 metres, I wondered just how this, at this distance and with this terrain, whether you really could see it.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good reading. I take it you look like a military person reading a map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Petrova Gora was both a location, but there is a tall building. In Serbian I believe "Gora" also means mountain or something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a building, a tall building like a tower. It's up, up the building. When you climb the building, which I did, where the radio station was located, you can see Zagreb from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would say from the radio tower which adds to the elevation.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You couldn't see it from the ground.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was there, I saw it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but you couldn't see it if you were not in the tower.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's clarified, why I didn't understand it. Well, these are my questions. Unless the questions of the Chamber would have raised any issue that the parties would like to further question the witness on, which is not the case. Mr. Kirudja, I'd like to thank you very much for testifying for a relatively long time answering questions of both parties and the Bench. I thank you very much for coming, and I wish you a safe trip -- I usually say a safe trip home, but I don't know where your next assignment will be, so a safe trip wherever you go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please accompany Mr. Kirudja out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would move for admission into evidence Prosecution exhibits 120 through 151.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Usually, Mr. Harmon, the registrar reads the, I would say, summaries, and that would take a considerable time with 31 exhibits. I therefore ask the registrar to give you an outprint of what she wrote down as the summarius description of the documents and rather than go through numbers than by reading all these descriptions. If that would be agreeable to the parties, I suggest the following: That the Chamber gives a decision on the admission of these documents, and if there would be anything in respect of the description of the document that in your view would need correction, we always could change the description, the exhibit still being admitted into evidence. That then would be the documents 120 up 'til 151. I make the following notes: Apart from Exhibits 121, 122, 123, and 124, which are all maps, whether or not annotated maps, all the other exhibits are accompanied by a translation into the non-original language, which always bears the same number but added to that .1. And I specify that in respect of P141, the original is already accompanied by a, as it was often said, poor translation into English, so 141 is the memorandum of Radomir Pasic in English and B/C/S of the 6th of July, 1992, whereas P141.1 is the -- I think, Madam Registrar, perhaps you'd look at it, is the translation to English where it reads "B/C/S translation." But that is the official translation, and that will be then corrected. It is the official translation of the original B/C/S document which was accompanied by an unofficial and poor translation. If there are no objections. Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, Your Honour. I wish you to continue and then I will raise a point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I wondered whether there were any objections against the P exhibits. There are no. If there are not, they are all admitted into evidence as I just explained. Then we have one Defence Exhibit, which is D15. It will be marked for identification at this very moment until we receive a final and official translation so that we have -- and we know that it's almost -- the translation is almost perfect. But for the time being, it will be marked for identification, Madam Registrar, under number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D15 ID.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have one question, and that is of course the exhibits that were tendered by the Prosecution often are multiple, separate documents. One is a cover sheet, one is a memorandum, and one is an attached document. I note, for example, in the description that is provided in 147, that exhibit contained a memorandum, a cover sheet -- I'm sorry, a cover sheet dated the 21st of July, it contained a separate memorandum, and it contained a separate letter from the Prime Minister of Croatia, Franjo Gregurevic. In the description of the list that I have been provided there is no such distinction made. I don't know to what extent the Court wants me to make suggestions to correct the list and be more precise. I'm satisfied, frankly, to have the exhibits as they were tendered be admitted. The list itself, I should not have to make suggestions and take the time to complete.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course if -- if you would not be satisfied with the description, of course you may make any suggestions for amending the description on the list. On the other hand, of course, finally, the documents, as they are in the hands of the registrar, are admitted into evidence, and I think on the basis of the transcript we always could look at what we actually looked at, because you usually introduced the document by saying we look at the front page and then attach this and this and this. But if not necessary, I would avoid to ask the registrar to give a more precise, more detailed description as given on the list at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just comment, Your Honour, that I'll just say at this moment that we don't feel completely comfortable with that but we will follow Your Honour's direction and go away and consider the question of what's an adequate description and then communicate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you are afraid of any confusion to arise, you always can make suggestion and Madam Registrar will certainly gladly amend on the basis your suggestion, but rather to go through everything and say there's a cover page attached, I think that's not even a level of detail we usually have if the descriptions are read out.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I just -- I just wanted to -- to indicate that we're not necessarily immediately a hundred per cent happy, but we won't be unnecessarily difficult about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any suggestion will be taken into consideration. But let's move on, because otherwise this new procedure takes more time than the efficient reading out by the registrar. Before we give an opportunity to the Prosecution to call its next witness, perhaps we should first go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I raise one other matter, Your Honour, which is this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- we have, of course -- of course we discussed with Mr. Krajisnik -- of course we meet Mr. Krajisnik regularly, and we Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. naturally discuss with him what happens in court and occasionally naturally have to explain to our client certain aspects of what happens in court. We also have to report, naturally, it's part of our duty, report and explain to Mr. Krajisnik anything which happens in -- at the meetings or sessions at which he's not present. We have had some difficulty and therefore would very much appreciate some clarification from the Tribunal. We have had difficulty in slightly in understanding ourselves but therefore difficulty in explaining to Mr. Krajisnik how it was that the -- this case, Krajisnik, appeared on the schedule which was published by the Tribunal on the 24th of May, which was last Monday, as listed for hearing on Monday morning, the 7th of June. I first saw that schedule later in the week, actually, I can't remember exactly when, but I think it was Thursday or Friday, and it was in general circulation, as that schedule is, of the various courtrooms. I now realise that on the 26th, so between the publication of that schedule and in fact, as it happens, when it came into my hands, the official spokesman for the Tribunal, and I think the Trial Chambers, I think that's the way he's described, had issued a press statement announcing - and it's on the website for the Tribunal - that the sentencing hearing for Mr. Babic would be at 10.00 a.m. on Monday the 7th, and this was alluded to by Your Honour, and you were able to give us a certain amount of information, but I think it's -- it was acknowledged not complete information in relation to this matter last Friday. But I would appreciate clarification, because as a matter of something affecting Mr. Krajisnik, and as it's slightly puzzling, I confess it is slightly puzzling to us what happened here, and I would appreciate any clarification. I have only realised over the weekend - I didn't know before because some things just pass me by - I had not realised that the identity of the Trial Chamber and in fact the three Judges dealing with Mr. Babic's sentencing hearing, when we had the meeting on Friday I'm afraid I didn't appreciate that Your Honours were the same Judges in relation to Mr. Babic as well, but I hope Your Honour sees that it would be helpful and set minds at rest if we were to understand how all that came about and what the -- what the arrangements have been, because I appreciate Your Honours are in that slightly difficult position of being, if you like, the Babic Trial Chamber with one hat on, as we say in English, but the Krajisnik Trial Chamber with another hat on, but, Your Honours are human beings, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- with one brain each.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much for establishing the fact rather than what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's just my evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd rather discuss that during -- we'll call the Babic Defence counsel, who has asked to be present, first because we call Mr. Babic in, and then I'd rather deal with that matter in his presence because --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That would seem to absolutely make sense that Mr. Mueller should be present in relation to this sort of matter, Your Honour. We agree with that, with respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stewart. Before we ask Mr. Mueller to come in, we have two issues. First of all, 89(F), the evidence which will be submitted under -- the written statement which will be submitted under Rule 89(F) can be expected to find no opposition from the Chamber. At the same time, the motion in respect of 92 bis, which I think the same matters 89(F) and 92 bis are dealt with in the same motion, we will not decide at this moment on the admission of the 92 bis evidence. We'll delay our decision until we have heard the viva voce testimony, especially since the Chamber gave some guidance as to how to -- to use statements or transcripts in relation to the viva voce evidence. So we'll not decide on that issue. Then I'd like Mr. Mueller to be accompanied into the courtroom. Mr. Mueller, welcome. Our apologies for the delay. Mr. Mueller, you have asked to be present during the testimony to be given by your client, Mr. Babic, in the Krajisnik case. You may be seated, it will take a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUELLER
utterances.text: You want me to be seated?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At this moment. I'm not saying -- at this moment, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUELLER
utterances.text: Okay. You want me to maybe -- the microphone. You want me to use the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't invite you yet to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUELLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have dealt with the situation before when another witness testified in this case, and we then spent a lot of attention to what would be the role of Defence counsel in respect of the witness. I've asked the Prosecution before whether there was any intention to prosecute Mr. Babic on new elements that would come up, and there's a commitment from the Prosecution that there is no intention whatsoever to come up with new indictments against Mr. Babic even if he would say a few matters which might be incriminating in respect of him. So therefore, that could hardly be a reason to -- to intervene. I also have to emphasise that of course a charge under a joint criminal enterprise covers a lot, so to start new proceedings on the basis that there's another -- that other charges should be brought against Mr. Babic is very unlikely to happen. Then in the -- it was about Mr. Deronjic. In the -- with Mr. Deronjic we also discussed whether he had to fear any prosecution by a domestic authority. At that time, there was a commitment by the Prosecution that they would prevent, to the extent possible, to support whatever domestic prosecution against the then-witness but then potential accused in the domestic system. The primary jurisdiction the Tribunal has certainly gives powers to prevent domestic jurisdictions to proceed against someone, of course as long as it concerns facts which are within the jurisdiction of this Tribunal. So therefore, if Mr. Babic, during his testimony, which I do not expect on the basis of his statement, suddenly confessed a horrible crime in 1988 in a third country, then of course the primary jurisdiction of the Tribunal could not protect him. But that's also an event which is very unlikely to happen. Finally, in -- prior to the testimony of Mr. Deronjic, we discussed whether -- whether his testimony could be unfavourable for the ongoing sentencing proceedings against at that time Mr. Deronjic, but the same might be true in respect of Mr. Babic. There was some discussion then as to whether Rule 90(E), which allows a witness to indicate that answering a question would incriminate himself would -- whether that would also be applicable if the answer would worsen his situation in view of sentencing. We then decided that we would cross that bridge as we came to it, and we didn't come to it at that time. So that's just for your information what the position is. We allowed at that time Defence counsel for Mr. Deronjic to be present but under the strict condition that he should clearly keep in mind the very, very limited -- the very, very limited circumstances under which the Chamber would -- oh, yes. You could have used -- I'm sorry, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUELLER
utterances.text: Much easier with the headphones on. Thank you. Much better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To clearly keep in mind the very limited circumstances under which the Chamber would consider any intervention appropriate. That's point one. And the second is that there would be no direct contact between the witness and counsel. That's the reason why I said for the time being I'll ask you to sit there, but as a matter of fact, I just -- there's a microphone also at the bench and this courtroom layout is a bit unfavourable, there are nicer solutions in other courtrooms, but I would invite you then to sit there, just next to the door, and to use that microphone if necessary. That's as far as the Rules are concerned in respect of your presence. Then we have another issue. That is -- I have two more issues. The first one is the Defence of Mr. Krajisnik has inquired into the court schedule since the published court schedule indicates that next Monday we would pronounce sentence against Mr. Babic and at the same time would hear the Krajisnik case. First of all, court scheduling is an administrative matter, but the Chamber has issued a Scheduling Order to pronounce the sentencing judgement against Mr. Babic next Monday, but that's not going any more. The parties -- you will be informed about it, it will be later. And just to -- to inform you that the reasons are mainly logistical ones. The Chamber is, of course, as you might not be surprised of, preparing the sentencing judgement, and as every experienced lawyer knows, that there are two issues: One is to make up your mind on the basis of all the arguments exchanged, and the second one is to get it on paper in such a way that it can be pronounced. I can assure you that the second issue is mainly on our minds at this moment, and together with logistical problems, the delivery of the sentencing judgement will be considerably delayed, as I said, both for logistical reasons and for finally finalising the decision. This answers to some -- so therefore it's not made public yet, but it will be made public either today or tomorrow that there will be no sentencing judgement delivered in the case of Mr. Babic next Monday. Mr. Stewart, this also, I would say, clarifies to some extent what you asked for.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, it does indeed. Thank you to -- with one or two caveats which are expressed in what Your Honour has said. This is a fast-moving situation as far as the Defence are concern. We've gathered all sorts of bits of information over the last two or three days in relation to the position of Mr. Babic. Talking about and putting it all together, two points do occur to us now. One is that in all the open sessions over the last week or so, there has been constant reference to Mr. Babic being the next witness. That has been said many, many times, and we have discussed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I checked it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- in quite some detail. Coupled with that, which seems to be the situation anyway, if Mr. Babic -- if the Krajisnik case is -- no disrespect to Mr. Krajisnik, I always refer to him as Mr. Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- but if the Krajisnik case is seen to be listed and heard on Monday in closed session, after two or three days of evidence with a witness in closed session, and Mr. Babic's sentencing hearing publicly announced by a press spokesman for the Tribunal last week as scheduled for Monday the 7th of June does not take place on that day, we simply ask, isn't it becoming blindingly obvious to anybody in the world outside with half a brain that it's Mr. Babic giving evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So what is this all about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Everyone who looks at the transcript of last Friday would know exactly when he was about to start, et cetera, but that decision has been taken, and we were aware of the whole of the public knowing -- that's also the reason why I asked Mr. Tieger just in the beginning whether it was just the fact that Mr. Babic would testify or not, but that's a matter which has been decided, and we will not reopen the debate on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Is the position this, Your Honour -- may I just ask this -- Mr. Mueller is in court, so perhaps it's appropriate to say it now -- clearly the Prosecution are -- I'm not resiling from the degree of non-opposition which I indicated to Mr. Tieger yesterday, it's just that we do see these other aspects of the matter coming along. Not all of them. The Trial Chamber no doubt was more fully aware of all these different elements than the Defence team has been because we've had to gather information as we go along. So that's why we make in effect these supplementary submissions. We understand entirely, of course, the Prosecution in their own interests and as their duty make these submissions and make these applications in relation to witnesses such as Mr. Babic, but we assume that, after all, it all stems from a request by Mr. Babic. We therefore suppose that in the end, now Mr. Babic is represented in court, that the continuation of this protection of Mr. Babic by closed session would only be thought to be necessary to continue so long as Mr. Babic, through his counsel, wished it to, and we understand that at the moment they do wish it to, but that, we understand, must be the position, that if at any point Mr. Babic through his counsel, who is now in court, were to say, "Well, it's pointless because it's going to be obvious," to Mr. Babic, then he would make that submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mueller, I'm addressing you now as -- I would say as counsel for a witness and not counsel of someone who still has to be sentenced in this Tribunal. The Defence is not informed about the facts underlying the motion of the Prosecution that ask for protective measures to the effect that Mr. Babic would testify in closed session. I just inform you about this before what we discussed during the long time would be, just become ineffective because of any of your remarks, but the question of the Defence of Mr. Krajisnik is whether you'd say, since everyone knows anyhow, at least could know on the basis of transcripts of public hearings, that Mr. Babic is testifying now, whether it still makes any sense or not to ask for the protective measures. If you would say, "We don't need them," fine, we'll hear it. If not, please tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUELLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the answer shall not be done within one phrase. We have learned about circumstances a couple of days ago which make it very reasonable that protective measures are taken -- are being taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but the explanation is clearly --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUELLER
utterances.text: Explanation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- is clearly in --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUELLER
utterances.text: Mr. Babic -- I'm sorry. I'm sorry. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUELLER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Babic is still insisting on protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUELLER
utterances.text: And I do not see any reason why I could circumvent his intention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUELLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear then, at least --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. That's unequivocally clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then finally I have another issue, and I waited with this until Mr. Mueller had arrived because it concerns him as well. Our court schedule for this week --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Trial Chamber has been exploring possibilities, also for logistical reasons, to sit longer during Thursday and Friday. As a matter of fact we would have preferred to sit an extra three hours on Thursday but I have just been informed this is not possible, but we could gain another one hour and a half tomorrow. Similar possibilities for Friday still have to be investigated first, whether there are teams of translators available. Therefore, if the parties would be unable to continue tomorrow in the afternoon for one and a half additional hours, I would like to be informed. That's point one. The second issue is that, when talking about Friday, Mr. Mueller, I am informed that you will not be available on Friday, but although the Chamber allows you to be present or to send someone to substitute you, the Chamber is not willing to adapt the court schedule where we have major problems in trying to finalise the testimony of the -- of Mr. Babic by next Monday, the Chamber is not willing to postpone the Friday hearing to any other moment. This doesn't affect the acceptance of the presence of a counsel for Mr. Babic, but your unavailability, however regrettable it may be, is not a reason for us to postpone the Friday session. Then having said all this, I think, Mr. Mueller, it would be the proper time to take your strategic position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUELLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And to ask Madam Usher to escort Mr. Babic into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, yes, the -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You invited you said -- you asked whether the parties would be unable to continue tomorrow in the afternoon for one and a half additional hours, you'd like to be informed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not beginning by saying that there is some physical unavailability of our team. There isn't. That's not a problem. We're here in The Hague. We seem to be here quite a lot. The -- but we do just wonder what the -- in the light particularly of the observations and discussions that took place last week about the form in which Mr. Babic's evidence would be presented --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- I know that this is also a fast-moving situation for Mr. Tieger. I wonder if Mr. Tieger is able just to give us a brief indication of where we think we might be going in terms of timetable on Mr. Babic, how long he's going to take in chief and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, without inviting you to speculate, if you could give information, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'll try to dampen my impulse to speculate and -- I -- I'm hoping that we can conclude the examination-in-chief within six hours. It's a bit difficult for me to assess the pace at which we'll move, but if that's -- I think it is at least a realistic prospect that we could conclude on Thursday so that Friday would be cross-examination. Now, my estimate may be more than partially off, but that's -- that's the fairest estimate I can make at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The reason, Your Honour, is this -- that's very helpful. We have been trying to do our scheduling, subject, of course, always to the Trial Chamber's directions and decisions. Up to a few minutes ago, I had been under the clear impression, as a result of discussions between the Prosecution and including Mr. Harmon and myself, and also knowing the position of Mr. Mueller, that we would -- excuse me -- that Mr. Biskovic would be the witness giving evidence on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that has been suggested, and when I saw that for the first time, and it was I think yesterday because we first had Mr. Babic on our list and there was no ruling yet on whether we would postpone or adopt to the schedule of Mr. Mueller, it may have been quite clear that -- well, even if it's not clear, the Chamber has given preference to first finish the testimony of Mr. Babic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I finish?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I understand, of course, that -- we know the Trial Chamber's position on that, and I suppose that everybody in principle likes to start from the position that it's better if a witness goes straight through from start to finish uninterrupted. That's normal court practice in the whole world, I think. But that was our understanding. We didn't understand from all the various discussions there'd been that there was any special difficulty then about Mr. Babic's evidence continuing on Monday. Your Honour's indicated something a moment ago which suggests that that's difficult. We did know that difficulties emerged then in the course of next week, and we understand those, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but there's always a risk. If I look at the -- if I look at the experience we have gained in respect of the examination of witnesses, there would be a risk that we might not conclude by Monday, and that's a risk I would at all costs want to avoid.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When Your Honour says "at all cost" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, of course not at all cost.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm not meaning to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I think during one of the meetings I hinted to -- I would say to the private agendas of Judges. I think I said something I might have to see my psychiatrist in Moscow, as you may have noticed. This was, of course, just an allusion to matters not to be discussed anywhere --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Of course. We understand that entirely. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and the Chamber wants, to the extent possible, hear the evidence of Mr. Babic by all three Judges. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would certainly wish that to be the position, naturally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but you know there are rules sometimes that allow for specific reasons one of the Judges not to be present but we want to avoid at all -- not at all cost but we certainly have a strong preference to hear the testimony of Mr. Babic with all three Judges, and I wouldn't know that if we wouldn't finish by Monday whether that would be possible. Let's leave it to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we could cross the bridge whether it might be appropriate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The earlier we start with the testimony of Mr. Babic, the better the chance.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour, but there are many, many difficulties in changing situations and bits of information that the Defence has had to cope with in relation to this, and the point I'm getting at is this: Your Honour, I do not know whether we will be ready to cross-examine Mr. Babic within this time scale, so when Your Honour says "at all costs," one of the costs which we always understand the Court would not regard as an acceptable cost is a cross-examination where the party was genuinely, for good reason, not ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me be quite clear: Last Friday we discussed when to start with the testimony of Mr. Babic; in the middle of this week. We also discussed whether we would be able to finish him next Friday or whether we would need Monday, and I think I clearly expressed I didn't hear anything at that moment as far as another witness is concerned. I was confronted with that, a change in order, a suggestion, only yesterday for the first time, so not only for the Defence matters are changing but sometimes for the Chamber as well. We want to start the testimony of Mr. Babic at this moment and we'll see where it ends, and it's for the first time that I'm confronted with this situation, but let's start and see where it ends. Madam Usher, could you please -- no, no. I think it's security who should escort Mr. Babic into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry. May I make one further observation which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- because -- which is this: It is so far as tomorrow afternoon is concerned. Part of the exercise of preparing for any witness, of course, and this applies to Mr. Babic, involves Mr. Krajisnik. When we add time to a hearing such as tomorrow, we also take away time from any spare capacity, of which there is virtually nil anyway in the Defence team, to consult Mr. Krajisnik. So, Your Honour, I must say I think I'm expressing this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- we are very unhappy about an extended day at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we would sit tomorrow in the afternoon there might be a suggestion to have an opportunity, and I'm just informed that the same would be possible on Friday, so I take it that during the lunch break Mr. Krajisnik would stay in this building if we would sit in the afternoon as well, which might give more opportunity to speak with Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is becoming oppressive. This is becoming distinctly oppressive. Mr. Krajisnik sits in court here as the defendant on trial for several hours a day, and to suggest that in relation to the voluminous material in relation to Mr. Babic, an important matter, that we then, in addition to everything else we have had to do and everything else Mr. Krajisnik has to do, that we are then to take that break, which for Mr. Krajisnik, apart from us, because we are deemed to be superhuman often for these purposes, though there are limits as far as counsel are concerned, but, Your Honour, we -- I think that's -- I've probably said enough now. I've registered the various points --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, you do not find my suggestion a good one. I do understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I think that's got across, thank you, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: All right, then Mr. Babic, who might be waiting, ready behind the door, can now enter the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, before giving evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. May I invite you to make that declaration. The text will be handed now to you by Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated, Mr. Babic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, we allowed to -- we allowed Mr. Mueller, your counsel, to be present in this courtroom. If you just look over all this paperwork there, you'll see he's sitting there. May I instruct you that that is also the last time you look at him, because you're supposed not to seek any contact, any direct contact, not even eye contact with Mr. Mueller. Mr. Mueller has been instructed on what his role could be. You could entirely leave it to Mr. Mueller. If there's at any moment a situation where you would like to seek the advice Mr. Mueller, although as the Chamber has explained to Mr. Mueller, there are hardly any situations imaginable where there would arise something that would ask anything else from you than just to give answer to the questions, but if such a moment would, nevertheless, in view of you arise, you may address me. You may not address Mr. Mueller directly. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Mr. Tieger:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Babic.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me quickly address a few background facts with you. You were born in 1956; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You obtained a medical education, studying dentistry in Belgrade, and you were appointed director of the health centre in Knin in Croatia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the period from 1990 through 1995, you occupied certain positions, political positions, in Croatia, and I'd like to enumerate those now and ask you at the end of that enumeration whether those are accurate. First you became a member of the regional committee of the Serbian Democratic Party, the SDS, for Krajina in February of 1990.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: For Knin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You later became -- you later became the president of the Main Committee in Knin, also in 1990. You became the president of the regional committee for Krajina. You occupied the position of the president of the Knin municipality for four years, beginning in 1990. You became president of the Association of Municipalities of Northern Dalmatia and Lika. You became president of the Serbian National Council, president of the Executive Council for SAO Krajina, the Serbian Autonomous District of Krajina. You became president of SAO Krajina in 1991, President of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, the RSK, in 1991 until February of 1992. You were president of the SDS party Croatia after the death of Jovan Raskovic. You were the minister of foreign affairs of the RSK in 1994 and were briefly the Prime Minister of RSK in 1995. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: It is correct, except that I wasn't the president of the SDS for Croatia but, rather, for Krajina. That's what it was called, the SDS for Krajina, not for the entire territory of Croatia. The rest is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 2001, is it correct that you contacted the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICTY after learning that you had been named in the indictment of Slobodan Milosevic and made that contact in order to explain your role in the events and to clear up the truth about that role and the events surrounding the war in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you participated in interviews with the Office of the Prosecutor at length without promises or immunity after you made contact with the OTP. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it also correct that on the 27th of January, 2004, you entered a plea of guilty to a crime against humanity, persecutions, for your participation in a joint criminal enterprise which had as its purpose the permanent forcible removal of the majority of the Croat and other non-Serb populations from approximately one-third of the territory of the Republic of Croatia in order to make it part of a new Serb-dominated state?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes, as described in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that plea was accepted by the court the following day, on the 28th of January; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time may I ask that the plea agreement and factual basis be marked Prosecution's next in order.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P152.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, just to inform you, since we have a bit of a different schedule today, I'd like to have a break at approximately quarter past twelve.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And may the exhibit be presented to the witness. I see it is being.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, do you recognise that document as the plea agreement and the factual basis in your case?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I do recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand it is the Court's practice to defer tendering of the exhibits until the conclusion of the examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, tendering, we usually give a decision at the end, but numbers are always attributed to the documents.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, next I'd like to place before you a document that was introduced in a case you testified in, the case involving Mr. Milosevic, and I'd like that marked next in order, which I believe would be P153. First of all, Mr. Babic, did you have an opportunity before your testimony in the Milosevic case to listen to a series of intercepted telephone conversations in order to determine whether you could identify the participants?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, quite a lot of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And does the document before you reflect your declaration that you had listened to the attached intercepted telephone conversations and identified the voices of the participants as indicated?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that a true and accurate declaration?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was. I apologise, but in the Serbian text it says that I was eavesdropping. I wasn't doing that. I was simply listening to them. The inference is a bit different in the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the English translation which you -- well, the English version which you signed states as you have indicated, that you listened to the following intercepted telephone conversations, and I advise you, therefore, that the clarification you offered is reflected in the English version which you did sign.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, next I'd like to have the witness presented with a copy of the statement which was submitted pursuant to 89(F). Your Honour, I ask that be marked. I believe it would be P154.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, is the document before you, Prosecution's number 154, a statement provided by you to the Office of the Prosecutor on the dates indicated?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you confirm that it is true and accurate?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, prior to -- prior to moving the statement into evidence, we'll provide the Court with binders of the attached intercepts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, we're going to ask you momentarily to set that document aside. You have had an opportunity to review the positions that you held in Knin and in Krajina during 1990 to 1995. Let me turn you for a moment to 1990 and ask if you attended the founding rally of the SDS party Croatia in February 1990?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it also correct that you joined the SDS believing that a new party was needed to represent the special interests of the region which was overwhelmingly Serb?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, in the Knin region.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the ensuing election, is it correct that the SDS party won a majority in four municipalities in Croatia, including your whole municipality of Knin, and after a second election, won a majority in another municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. The second round of elections, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that in July of 1990 the SDS party in Bosnia and Herzegovina was founded?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, on St. Peter's Day, which is celebrated in the Orthodox church.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did the head of the Croatian SDS party, Dr. Jovan Raskovic, support the Bosnian SDS party during its electoral campaign?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes. The election of the president of the SDS in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Dr. Karadzic, as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, was there an initial conflict or dispute about the membership of the parties in different municipalities in Bosnian Krajina, or Bosanska Krajina, which was resolved with the decision that those committees would belong to SDS Bosnia-Herzegovina rather than SDS Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And later in 1993, was there an effort to unite the SDS parties of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia and Serbia and Montenegro under the leadership of Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the outcome of that effort?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Well, most of the SDS branches united into one SDS of all Serb lands under the leadership of Dr. Karadzic except for the one whose president I was. Our party did not join this united SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe we've reached the moment for adjournment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we did, Mr. Tieger. We will adjourn until twenty-five minutes to one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before we continue, we will sit tomorrow in the afternoon for one and a half hour, and whatever assistance the Defence would need in order to find ways to facilitate the communication with Mr. Krajisnik, not only during the lunch break but in whatever way, the Chamber is -- will only be too glad to assist to the extent possible. That's point one. Friday would be the same. And tomorrow, but we will still have to look at this, there would even be an opportunity to sit three -- perhaps would be an opportunity to sit during three hours in the afternoon. That would be depend on the canceling of another case tomorrow in the afternoon. That's highly uncertain, so therefore for the moment it's one and a half hours extra, from 2.30 to 4.00 on Thursday and the same on Friday. At this point, there is another issue, and, Mr. Mueller, I would like you to clearly listen to this. If for any reason it would be preferable to have - and the same is, of course, true for the parties - if there would be any reason to make not public any part of the statement -- of the testimony of Mr. Babic for other reasons than the one why we are sitting in closed session, for example, personal matters or whatever reason there would be to keep certain aspects of his testimony confidential, the Chamber would like to be informed about it prior to giving a decision that the protective measures are lifted, because now nothing will be public but once the protective measure of closed session will be lifted, then everything would automatically be public, and if there are specific portions which for whatever reason should remain confidential, then of course we should not only lift the protective measure but also put in place for smaller portions protective measures. That's whether asked by the Defence or the Prosecution. There is a risk that we might overlook, since everything is confidential now, that we might overlook that perhaps smaller portions should remain. This is sort of a suggestion just to avoid whatever mistake at a later stage. Then Mr. Babic may -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just say something? On the first point Your Honour made, yes, there would be -- I don't know whether it is something that the Trial Chamber can help on, but we are having difficulty finding time to see Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the -- in the Detention Unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: At the Detention Unit tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll see whether we can solve that problem. If after this court hearing we could be informed, then we'll try to do whatever we can. So write down what the problem is, perhaps in one or two lines, and write down what your wishes would be and we'll see whether we could solve this problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And the only other point I will make, and I'll keep it very, very short, particularly in light of the fact the witness is already in court, the potential difficulty which I mentioned about 45 minutes ago, to put it as a piece of English understatement is certainly not made any less difficult by the proposals that the Trial Chamber has just put forward for the next two days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber is aware of that. Mr. Tieger, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, before we adjourned, you had referred to the establishment of the SDS Croatia and the subsequent formation of the SDS in Bosnia and Herzegovina, both in 1990. Did these events occur at a time when there was increasing concern about the potential disintegration of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you familiar or did you become familiar - excuse me - with the position of Slobodan Milosevic regarding the status of Serbs and the position to be taken by Serbs in the event of the dissolution of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us what that was, please.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: The position was that all Serbs -- that Serbs have the right to remain within Yugoslavia, in one state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, I'd like you next to look at a map that I would ask to have marked as Prosecution's next in order, including an accompanying translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P155.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I be excused [Realtime transcript read in error "executed"] from court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The record says that you will be executed from Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I thought it would come to that as well, frankly, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, we'll see you back later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, before I ask you specific questions about the map, it may be helpful simply to indicate what it depicts in a more general manner. First of all, is it correct that the upper portion of the map, including the block that extends down to the bottom of the page at the left, depicts the territory of the Republic of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the block we see in the middle of the map at the lower portion, does that indicate the territorial situation of Serbs in Croatia according to suburbs, done with regard to the census carried out on March 31, 1981?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning next to the block next to it, which is depicted in yellow at the lower -- at the lower portion of the map to the right side but excluding the legend at the bottom, is that indicated as a map of the Ustasha genocide upon the people of Serbia on the territory of the Independent State of Croatia between the years of 1941 and 1945?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the points depicted on the map are various points of genocide committed by Ustashas, concentration camps, and so on?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And turning finally to the block at the lower right-hand portion of the map, which is presently shown on screen, does that indicate the population of Krajina in numbers?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as of 1993, as indicated by the italicised portion at the bottom of the second column?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me focus your attention on that particular block for just a moment. Looking first at the first indicated area in the upper left-hand portion of that small block, Eastern Slavonia, Western Srem, and Baranja, does it indicate the democratic composition of that area in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that would be 95 per cent Serbs, 4 per cent Croats, and 1 per cent others?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning quickly to some of the others. Banija, which is listed below, is that 97 per cent Serb, 2 per cent Croat, and 1 per cent others?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Kordun, 98 per cent Serb, 2 per cent Croat?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And quickly, Lika an Northern Dalmatia have, respectively, 93 per cent Serb, 5 per cent Croat, 2 per cent others; and Northern Dalmatia 90 per cent Serb and 10 per cent others.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just in relation to this map and the evidence that's being adduced, it's not immediately apparent if Mr. Babic is in a position -- from what position he comments in relation to the demography. I don't believe a foundation has been laid for any expertise in relation to population numbers in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me ask a couple of questions in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Babic, do you know who produced this map?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
